# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".

B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

## 1. The toll

In 2023, gun violence killed 46,728 Americans. That is one person every 11 minutes, a death toll that did not pause for holidays, school hours or the dinner hour. Behind every one of those numbers is a name: a parent who will not be at the table, a student who will not graduate, a neighbor whose absence reshapes an entire block.

They leave families carrying funeral costs, medical debt and grief that does not resolve on anyone's schedule. And every one of them is counted in the federal data that Congress has the power to act on.

What makes this toll so corrosive is how much of it is preventable. The United States does not have a monopoly on mental illness, video games or social division. It does have two gaps in federal law that no comparable country tolerates: gun sales that proceed with no background check at all, and a market in assault weapons that the federal government stopped regulating in 2004. Close those gaps and the toll comes down. Leave them open and the country will read the same numbers again next year, with the same names attached.

It means pediatric emergency departments that plan for gunshot wounds the way they plan for flu season. It means parents who calculate which entrance of a mall is closest to the door, and coaches who know where the nearest exit is from any field. American childhood now carries a gunshot death rate that no other wealthy nation would accept for its own children, and no parent in those nations is asked to accept it.

Both of the gaps this brief addresses reach children directly. Guns acquired without a background check are the guns most likely to be transferred again and again, untraced, until one of them reaches a person who should never have had one. And assault weapons are the firearms built to maximize casualties in the shortest possible time, which is precisely the design brief of someone who walks into a school, a workplace or a bowling alley intending to kill as many people as possible. A country that can see this clearly in its own mortality data has no excuse for looking away.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed firearm dealer completes a sale. That system is simple, fast and familiar, and it does exactly what it was designed to do: stop sales to people who are legally prohibited from owning a gun.

The problem is that it only covers part of the market. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged between strangers online, at gun shows and through informal networks sit outside the system entirely, which means the same person a licensed dealer would have to turn away can find a willing seller in an afternoon. The result is a two-tier firearms market: one tier where the law asks questions, and a second tier where it asks none. For a prohibited purchaser, the second tier is not a loophole. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks legislation closes that second tier. It does not create a new system; it extends the check that licensed dealers already run to every sale, so that the question a dealer must ask is the question everyone must ask. States that have done this have shown that the policy works as a matter of administration, with checks completed in minutes and lawful commerce continuing.

This is also the most broadly supported gun safety policy in American politics. Support for background checks crosses party lines, crosses regions and crosses gun-owning households, because the underlying principle is one that gun owners and non-owners alike accept: if you are legally allowed to buy a firearm, a background check costs you nothing but a few minutes. The only people a background check slows down are the people the law already says cannot buy a gun. Congress is not being asked to take a risk here. It is being asked to finish a job it started in 1994.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023 there were 656 mass shootings in the United States, shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston. Those 656 shootings left 712 people dead, in the places Americans go to be together: schools, workplaces, grocery stores, dance halls, a weekday bowling league.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. That is not a rhetorical point; it is a design fact. These are semi-automatic firearms built around detachable, high-capacity magazines, configured to fire rapidly, accept accessories and deliver a lethal volume of fire without pausing to reload. A shooter with a hunting rifle has to work for casualties. A shooter with an assault weapon does not, and the difference shows up in the number of people who die in the minutes before anyone can intervene.

The federal government has already acknowledged this once. The assault weapons ban enacted in 1994 lapsed in 2004, and the firearms industry has spent the years since building the category back up and marketing it hard. Reinstituting the ban means writing the definition by function rather than by brand name: semi-automatic operation, detachable magazines, and the specific features that make these firearms convertible into weapons optimized for firing on people. Mass shootings are not the whole of gun violence, and this brief does not pretend otherwise. But they are the episodes in which the country watches, in real time, what its own policy choices produce. When the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings is a firearm that Congress once restricted and then let back onto the market, the response is not complicated. It is overdue.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Congress should write a new ban that defines assault weapons by their functional features, covers high-capacity magazines and replaces the restrictions that lapsed in 2004.

4. **Help states enact extreme-risk laws.** Congress should provide grants and technical assistance to states adopting extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and should fund the training that makes those laws work in practice.

They are a count of the cost of two open gaps in federal law, and the children shot and killed at 5.9 per 100,000 are the clearest measure of what that cost buys. ## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed firearm dealer completes a sale. That system is simple, fast and familiar, and it does exactly what it was designed to do: stop sales to people who are legally prohibited from owning a gun.

The problem is that it only covers part of the market. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged between strangers online, at gun shows and through informal networks sit outside the system entirely, which means the same person a licensed dealer would have to turn away can find a willing seller in an afternoon. The result is a two-tier firearms market: one tier where the law asks questions, and a second tier where it asks none. For a prohibited purchaser, the second tier is not a loophole. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks legislation closes that second tier. It does not create a new system; it extends the check that licensed dealers already run to every sale, so that the question a dealer must ask is the question everyone must ask. States that have done this have shown that the policy works as a matter of administration, with checks completed in minutes and lawful commerce continuing.

This is also the most broadly supported gun safety policy in American politics. Support for background checks crosses party lines, crosses regions and crosses gun-owning households, because the underlying principle is one that gun owners and non-owners alike accept: if you are legally allowed to buy a firearm, a background check costs you nothing but a few minutes. The only people a background check slows down are the people the law already says cannot buy a gun. Congress is not being asked to take a risk here. It is being asked to finish a job it started in 1994.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023 there were 656 mass shootings in the United States, shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston. Those 656 shootings left 712 people dead, in the places Americans go to be together: schools, workplaces, grocery stores, dance halls, a weekday bowling league.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. That is not a rhetorical point; it is a design fact. These are semi-automatic firearms built around detachable, high-capacity magazines, configured for rapid fire and accessorizing, and designed to deliver a lethal volume of rounds without pausing to reload. That is what makes it possible for one shooter to take so many lives in the minutes before anyone can intervene, and it is why the casualty counts in America's mass shootings look the way they do.

The federal government has already acknowledged this once. The assault weapons ban enacted in 1994 lapsed in 2004, and the firearms industry has spent the years since building the category back up and marketing it hard. Reinstituting the ban means writing the definition by function rather than by brand name: semi-automatic operation, detachable magazines, and the specific features that make these firearms convertible into weapons optimized for firing on people. An updated ban should also address the high-capacity magazines that drive casualty counts, and it should be paired with the background check system described above, because the two policies reinforce each other.

Mass shootings are not the whole of gun violence, and this brief does not pretend otherwise. But they are the episodes in which the country watches, in real time, what its own policy choices produce. When the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings is a firearm that Congress once restricted and then let back onto the market, the response is not complicated. It is overdue.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Congress should extend the background check requirement that already applies to licensed dealers to every firearm sale, so that no gun sale in the United States proceeds without one. This is the single most direct way to close the 40% of gun sales that take place without a background check.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Congress should write a new ban that defines assault weapons by their functional features, covers high-capacity magazines and replaces the restrictions that lapsed in 2004.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH.** Congress should provide dedicated, multiyear funding for gun violence prevention research, so that the next set of policy decisions is built on evidence rather than on the data we happen to have.

4. **Help states enact extreme-risk laws.** Congress should provide grants and technical assistance to states adopting extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and should fund the training that makes those laws work in practice.

## Closing the gaps

The 46,728 Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 are not an argument about culture. They are a count of the cost of two open gaps in federal law, and the children shot and killed at 5.9 per 100,000 are the clearest measure of what that cost buys. Congress knows how to close both gaps. It has done parts of each before, and the only thing that has changed since is the number of names.

*Data supporting every figure in this brief are documented in the accompanying data appendix.*

## 1. The toll

In 2023, gun violence killed 46,728 Americans. That is one person every 11 minutes, a death toll that did not pause for holidays, school hours or the dinner hour. Behind every one of those numbers is a name: a parent who will not be at the table, a student who will not graduate, a neighbor whose absence reshapes an entire block.

These deaths are not spread evenly, and they are not absorbed quietly. They land in classrooms and emergency rooms, at family celebrations and weekend gatherings, in big cities and in small towns. They leave families carrying funeral costs, medical debt and grief that does not resolve on anyone's schedule. And every one of them is counted in the federal data that Congress has the power to act on.

What makes this toll so corrosive is how much of it is preventable. The United States does not have a monopoly on mental illness, video games or social division. It does have two gaps in federal law that no comparable country tolerates: gun sales that proceed with no background check at all, and a market in assault weapons that the federal government stopped regulating in 2004. Close those gaps and the toll comes down. Leave them open and the country will read the same numbers again next year, with the same names attached.

## 2. America's children are being shot and killed

No figure in this brief is harder to read than the one on children. America's children are shot and killed at a rate of 5.9 per 100,000. Guns are the leading cause of death for America's children, ahead of car crashes, ahead of cancer, ahead of every disease and every other injury that parents have learned to fear on their children's behalf.

Sit with what that means in practice. It means a generation of students who have practiced lockdown drills before they learned long division. It means pediatric emergency departments that plan for gunshot wounds the way they plan for flu season. It means parents who calculate which entrance of a mall is closest to the door, and coaches who know where the nearest exit is from any field. American childhood now carries a gunshot death rate that no other wealthy nation would accept for its own children, and no parent in those nations is asked to accept it.

Both of the gaps this brief addresses reach children directly. Guns acquired without a background check are the guns most likely to be transferred again and again, untraced, until one of them reaches a person who should never have had one. And assault weapons are the firearms built to maximize casualties in the shortest possible time, which is precisely the design brief of someone who walks into a school, a workplace or a bowling alley intending to kill as many people as possible. A country that can see this clearly in its own mortality data has no excuse for looking away.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a licensed firearm dealer completes a sale. That system is simple, fast and familiar, and it does exactly what it was designed to do: stop sales to people who are legally prohibited from owning a gun.

The problem is that it only covers part of the market. 40% of gun sales take place without a background check. Sales arranged between strangers online, at gun shows and through informal networks sit outside the system entirely, which means the same person a licensed dealer would have to turn away can find a willing seller in an afternoon. The result is a two-tier firearms market: one tier where the law asks questions, and a second tier where it asks none. For a prohibited purchaser, the second tier is not a loophole. It is the whole point.

Universal background checks legislation closes that second tier. It does not create a new system; it extends the check that licensed dealers already run to every sale, so that the question a dealer must ask is the question everyone must ask. States that have done this have shown that the policy works as a matter of administration, with checks completed in minutes and lawful commerce continuing.

This is also the most broadly supported gun safety policy in American politics. Support for background checks crosses party lines, crosses regions and crosses gun-owning households, because the underlying principle is one that gun owners and non-owners alike accept: if you are legally allowed to buy a firearm, a background check costs you nothing but a few minutes. The only people a background check slows down are the people the law already says cannot buy a gun. Congress is not being asked to take a risk here. It is being asked to finish a job it started in 1994.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023 there were 656 mass shootings in the United States, shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston. Those 656 shootings left 712 people dead, in the places Americans go to be together: schools, workplaces, grocery stores, dance halls, a weekday bowling league.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. That is not a rhetorical point; it is a design fact. These are semi-automatic firearms built around detachable, high-capacity magazines, configured for rapid fire and accessorizing, and designed to deliver a lethal volume of rounds without pausing to reload. That is what makes it possible for one shooter to take so many lives in the minutes before anyone can intervene, and it is why the casualty counts in America's mass shootings look the way they do.

The federal government has already acknowledged this once. The assault weapons ban enacted in 1994 lapsed in 2004, and the firearms industry has spent the years since building the category back up and marketing it hard. Reinstituting the ban means writing the definition by function rather than by brand name: semi-automatic operation, detachable magazines, and the specific features that make these firearms convertible into weapons optimized for firing on people. An updated ban should also address the high-capacity magazines that drive casualty counts, and it should be paired with the background check system described above, because the two policies reinforce each other.

Mass shootings are the moments when the country watches, in real time, what its own policy choices produce. When the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings is a firearm that Congress once restricted and then let back onto the market, the response is not complicated. It is overdue.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Congress should extend the background check requirement that already applies to licensed dealers to every firearm sale, so that no gun sale in the United States proceeds without one. This is the single most direct way to close the gap created by the 40% of gun sales that take place without a background check.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Congress should write a new ban that defines assault weapons by their functional features, covers high-capacity magazines and replaces the restrictions that lapsed in 2004.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH.** Congress should provide dedicated, multiyear funding for gun violence prevention research, so that the next set of policy decisions is built on evidence rather than on the data we happen to have.

4. **Help states enact extreme-risk laws.** Congress should provide grants and technical assistance to states adopting extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and should fund the training that makes those laws work in practice.

## Closing the gaps

The 46,728 Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 are not an argument about culture. They are a count of the cost of two open gaps in federal law, and the children shot and killed at 5.9 per 100,000 are the clearest measure of what that cost buys. Congress knows how to close both gaps. It has done parts of each before, and the only thing that has changed since is the number of names.
